title: Understanding Learner-LLM Chatbot Interactions and the Impact of Prompting Guidelines
extended_summary:
This paper examines how novice learners interact with large language model (LLM) chatbots and whether structured prompting guidance improves the quality of those interactions. The authors focus on a common problem in AI-assisted learning: users often struggle to write effective prompts, which can lead to vague, inefficient, or low-quality chatbot responses. The study also explores how user behavior during chatbot conversations can be systematically analyzed using the Von NeuMidas annotation framework.

The intervention was an online educational experiment in which participants first completed an introductory AI literacy video and then interacted with ChatGPT on a learning task about the threats and mechanisms of social media. After this initial phase, participants were randomly assigned to one of three prompting-guideline conditions: (1) a task-specific guideline set designed by the authors, (2) a prompt-pattern-based set derived from prior literature, and (3) a simpler task-specific set generated by ChatGPT. Participants then received training with descriptions and examples for their assigned strategy and completed additional chatbot interactions on the same task. The study combined quantitative analyses of prompt success and task success with manual and LLM-assisted annotation of dialogue features and prompting behaviors.

The population consisted of 107 adults aged 18-32, recruited through Prolific and residing in the UK or USA. Participants were selected for limited prior experience with ChatGPT, making the sample representative of novice rather than expert AI users. The study was conducted online through a custom interface connected to the ChatGPT API, and it generated 642 interactions and 4,536 exchanged messages for analysis.

The main conclusion is that prompting training significantly improved participants' ability to craft successful prompts and improved the overall quality of human-LLM conversations. However, the study did not find statistically significant differences between the three prompting-guideline approaches, likely because of overlap among the guideline features and unequal group sizes. The authors argue that structured prompting instruction can strengthen AI literacy and make learner-chatbot interactions more purposeful and effective, while also showing that the Von NeuMidas annotation scheme is useful for analyzing changes in interaction behavior beyond a single task context.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's large language model chatbot used for natural-language conversational assistance and instruction.
identified_tools.use_case: Participants with limited prior ChatGPT experience used a custom interface connected to the ChatGPT API to have ChatGPT act as a personal teacher explaining threats and mechanisms of social media; the study tested whether different prompting-guideline trainings improved prompt quality, task success, and interaction behavior.

findings.finding_summary: Across 107 participants and 642 interactions, training produced a statistically significant improvement in prompt success, indicating participants became better at crafting successful prompts for ChatGPT after instruction. Repeated-measures ANOVA showed a main effect of training on prompt success, F(1, 93) = 8.447, p = .005, η² = 0.083; no significant training-by-guideline interaction was found, F(2, 93) = 0.198, p = .821, η² = 0.004.
findings.measure: Prompt success based on annotated features indicating adherence to the task and successful prompt formulation

findings.finding_summary: Training significantly improved task success, meaning the overall quality of the human-LLM conversations for the educational activity increased after participants received prompting-guideline instruction. Repeated-measures ANOVA showed a main effect of training on task success, F(1, 104) = 10.237, p = .002, η² = .090; the interaction between training and prompting-guideline condition was not significant, F(2, 104) = 0.128, p = .880, η² = .002.
findings.measure: Task success based on annotated features indicating whether the interaction achieved the intended learning activity

findings.finding_summary: All three prompting-guideline groups showed post-training behavioral improvements aligned with their assigned strategies, such as increased use of one-step instructions and topic specificity for ChatGPT-generated guidelines, greater use of flipped patterns for pattern guidelines, and more detailed task descriptions, role-play, and role-form/context requests for task-specific guidelines. However, the paper reports no statistically significant differences between the three prompting strategies in overall prompt success or task success.
findings.measure: Adoption frequency of prompting-guideline features in user prompts; between-guideline differences in success outcomes

findings.finding_summary: Von NeuMidas annotations indicated that after training, users interacted with ChatGPT in a more directive and structured way, with increased user-issued directions, more social conventions, and a general increase in Von NeuMidas command types, especially output commands. The authors interpret this as evidence of a more intentional and goal-oriented interaction style after prompting training, though no inferential statistics were reported for these annotation shifts.
findings.measure: Von NeuMidas/MIDAS interaction-quality annotation features before vs. after training

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical pre/post educational experiment with random assignment to prompting-guideline groups, but it does not report a control group without training and focuses on annotated interaction outcomes rather than standardized academic achievement. The design supports suggestive causal claims about training effects, but methodological limitations keep it below green.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports statistically significant positive training effects with small-to-moderate eta-squared values (η²=.083 and .090), but effects are on prompt/task success annotations rather than direct learning achievement and no guideline outperformed the others. Overall impact is positive but still somewhat unclear for student learning outcomes.
